rationale: Both responses have modelling flaws, but A identifies the mechanism that actually explains why the same technique sometimes gives 1.8x and sometimes slows down. A verify pass over K tokens costs about one decode step when decode is memory-bound, but about K steps once batch size or model size makes it compute-bound, where speculation cannot pay off. A makes this verify-cost ratio (gamma) the central variable and ties it to arithmetic intensity and batch size. Its proposed first experiment, timing a K-token forward pass against a 1-token pass at the serving batch size, is cheap, decisive and needs no draft head. A has errors: batch-1 decode of a 70B model is still memory-bound, its B* formula is dimensionally off, and its entropy-based ceiling on acceptance is heuristic. B's model is more seriously wrong. It sets the verify cost equal to a single-token pass, declares the speedup batch-independent and concludes that almost any acceptance rate pays off, so it cannot explain the observed slowdowns. Its 'hard upper bound' of mean target top-1 probability on acceptance is incorrect, since a perfect draft is accepted with probability 1. B's point about heterogeneous acceptance within a batch is a good one. Overall A's economics are sounder and more actionable.
